references.name: Amos Tversky
references.desc:
Kahneman’s fourteen-year collaborator. Co-author of the 1974
Science paper and prospect theory. The book is substantially a
memorial.

references.name: Richard Thaler
references.desc:
Nudge, Misbehaving. Mental accounting, endowment
effect, Save More Tomorrow. Founder of behavioral economics as a field.

references.name: Cass Sunstein
references.desc:
Nudge, availability cascades, punitive damages research,
Obama administration regulator.

references.name: Nassim Nicholas Taleb
references.desc:
The Black Swan, Fooled by Randomness. Narrative
fallacy, hindsight, the critique of economists’ overconfidence.

references.name: Paul Slovic
references.desc:
Affect heuristic, probability neglect, public risk perception,
denominator neglect.

references.name: Gary Klein
references.desc:
Naturalistic decision making, recognition-primed decisions, the
premortem. Long-running interlocutor and co-author with Kahneman on
when to trust expert intuition.

references.name: Paul Meehl
references.desc:
Clinical versus Statistical Prediction (1954). The
foundational case for algorithms over experts.

references.name: Robyn Dawes
references.desc:
Statistical prediction work; the “broken leg” rule;
first subject to take the Tom W test.

references.name: Philip Tetlock
references.desc:
Expert Political Judgment. Experts barely beat chance on
long-range political forecasts; hedgehogs do worse than foxes.

references.name: Daniel Gilbert
references.desc:
Stumbling on Happiness. Miswanting, affective forecasting,
the bias toward initial belief.

references.name: Ed Diener
references.desc:
Life satisfaction research; the Jen duration-neglect study;
subjective well-being measurement.

references.name: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
references.desc: Concept of flow; experience sampling methodology.

references.name: Roy Baumeister
references.desc: Ego depletion; glucose as substrate for self-control.

references.name: Walter Mischel
references.desc: The marshmallow test; self-regulation in children.

references.name: Keith Stanovich and Richard West
references.desc:
The System 1 / System 2 terminology; the algorithmic vs. reflective
mind distinction.

references.name: Matthew Rabin
references.desc:
The theorem proving expected utility incompatible with observed
risk aversion at small stakes.

references.name: Daniel Bernoulli
references.desc:
Original expected-utility framework (18th century); the theory
Kahneman and Tversky displaced.

references.name: Harry Markowitz
references.desc:
First proposed gains-and-losses framework for risky choice twenty-five
years before prospect theory.

references.name: Herbert Simon
references.desc: Defined expert intuition as recognition; bounded rationality.

references.name: Bent Flyvbjerg
references.desc:
Reference-class forecasting; cost overruns in large infrastructure
projects.

references.name: Michael Lewis
references.desc:
Moneyball, used throughout as the paradigmatic story of
data beating intuition.

references.name: Antonio Damasio
references.desc:
Descartes’ Error. Somatic marker hypothesis; emotion
as essential to decision.

references.name: Jonathan Haidt
references.desc:
“The emotional tail wags the rational dog.” Moral
judgment as emotion with rationalization appended.

references.name: Gerd Gigerenzer
references.desc:
Kahneman’s most persistent critic; “fast and frugal”
heuristics emphasize accuracy where K&T emphasize bias.

references.name: Phil Rosenzweig
references.desc:
The Halo Effect; the critique of business success
narratives like In Search of Excellence.

references.name: John Bargh
references.desc: Florida effect; priming research.

references.name: Kathleen Vohs
references.desc: Money priming and individualism.

references.name: Francis Galton
references.desc: Discovery of regression to the mean.

references.name: Virginia Apgar
references.desc: The Apgar score for newborn assessment.

references.name: Terry Odean
references.desc: Trading underperformance data; “Boys Will Be Boys.”

references.name: Maurice Allais
references.desc:
The 1952 paradox that first exposed violations of expected utility
theory.

references.name: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern
references.desc: Expected utility theory as formalized in the mid-twentieth century.

connections.title: The Hour Between Dog and Wolf
connections.author: John Coates

The Little Book of
        Market Wizards
connections.author: Jack Schwager
